summary: Analyzes the security of the BGP/MPLS IP VPN architecture of RFC 4364 for service providers and VPN users. It concludes that such networks can be as secure as layer-2 VPN services using ATM or Frame Relay. The document is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A safety inspection of a kind of private network, concluding it is about as safe as older private lines.

questions: how does mpls vpn separate traffic
subtitle: Security analysis of label-based private networks for service providers.

tldr.problem: Service providers and enterprises need to know whether BGP/MPLS IP VPNs offer the same security as traditional layer-2 VPN services like ATM and Frame Relay, and what security limitations exist.
tldr.mechanism: This document analyzes the BGP/MPLS IP VPN architecture against security requirements for VPNs: address and traffic separation, hiding of core infrastructure, resistance to attacks, and prevention of label spoofing. It examines advanced architectures like Carriers' Carrier and inter-provider connections.
tldr.outcome: The analysis concludes that BGP/MPLS IP VPNs can achieve security equivalent to ATM and Frame Relay VPNs when correctly configured, but also identifies limitations such as vulnerability to misconfiguration, lack of built-in encryption, and assumptions about core network trustworthiness.

today: RFC 4381 is an informational security analysis that remains relevant for operators and architects designing VPN services. It provides the authoritative assessment that BGP/MPLS IP VPNs achieve security comparable to traditional layer-2 VPN technologies when correctly configured.

sections.title: VPN Security Requirements
sections.content:
Virtual private networks (VPNs) must meet several security requirements. First, non-overlapping VPNs must maintain independent address spaces. For example, two VPNs should both be able to use 10.0.0.0/8 without conflict. Traffic from one VPN must never enter another VPN, and routing information must be kept separate per VPN.

Second, the internal structure of the provider's network should not be visible from outside. While obscurity alone is not security, operators prefer that attackers not know router addresses in the core. Third, the VPN must resist both denial-of-service attacks (where resources become unavailable to authorized users) and intrusions (where unauthorized users gain access).

Fourth, attackers must not be able to spoof (forge) MPLS labels to gain access to other VPNs. Finally, many existing VPN deployments do not encrypt traffic, but when confidentiality is required, encryption should be available. This analysis assumes the provider's core network is trusted and secure, so it does not address attacks by someone with access to core network elements.
sections.plainLanguage: A private network must keep each customer's data separate, hide how the network is built from outsiders, protect against attacks, and stop packets with fake labels from sneaking into the wrong place.

sections.title: Address Space and Traffic Separation
sections.content:
BGP/MPLS IP VPNs achieve address separation by adding a 64-bit Route Distinguisher (RD) to each IPv4 route, creating a VPN-IPv4 address that is unique across the entire MPLS core. This allows customers to use the same IP addresses in different VPNs and even in the core network.

Each Provider Edge (PE) router maintains a separate Virtual Routing and Forwarding instance (VRF) for each connected VPN. A VRF contains the routes of that VPN plus the addresses of peer PE routers. Since each VPN has its own VRF, there is no interference between VPNs on the PE router.

Across the core, routing separation is maintained using Route Distinguishers. VPN routes are exchanged exclusively between PE routers via Multi-Protocol BGP (MP-BGP), not distributed to the core. On the data plane, traffic separation is achieved by prepending a VPN-specific label to packets at the ingress PE; at the egress PE, the VPN label selects the correct egress VRF.

The architecture offers the same security as a layer-2 VPN: it is impossible to intrude from one VPN or the core into another VPN unless explicitly configured. Confidentiality (encryption) is not a standard MPLS VPN service but can be overlaid if required.
sections.plainLanguage: Each customer gets their own routing table and the packets get a special label that tells the network which customer they belong to. Labels are assigned only by PE routers, so nobody can fake a label from outside.

sections.title: Core Hiding and Address Obscurity
sections.content:
MPLS does not reveal unnecessary information to the outside world. The addressing of the core can use private addresses (RFC 1918) or public addresses. Since the interface to VPNs and the Internet is BGP, no internal information needs to be revealed. If dynamic routing is not required between Customer Edge (CE) and PE routers, static routing on unnumbered interfaces can hide the PE address entirely.

In a pure VPN-only network (no Internet access), information hiding is as good as on Frame Relay or ATM networks. No addressing information is revealed to third parties. If a customer chooses to access the Internet via the MPLS core, they must reveal the same information as any normal Internet service. Network Address Translation (NAT) can provide additional obscurity. Core routers should filter packets destined to the core infrastructure so they are unreachable from outside, making attacks very difficult even if addresses are known.

A BGP/MPLS IP VPN network with Internet access must reveal at least one IP address (of the peering PE router) to the upstream provider and thus to the outside world. Internet-connected networks face the same security threats as any Internet service and require appropriate defensive measures like firewalls and intrusion detection systems.
sections.plainLanguage: You can hide the network structure by not advertising internal router addresses, using private IP addresses for the core, and filtering packets aimed at the core. It is like keeping your phone number unlisted.

sections.title: Resistance to Attacks
sections.content:
Direct intrusion from one VPN to another is impossible due to address and traffic separation. However, an attacker might try to attack the MPLS core itself. Since the core addressing is hidden, an attacker cannot know the IP address of any internal router. The only reachable addresses from a VPN or the Internet are the peering addresses of PE routers.

If static routing with unnumbered interfaces is used, the PE interface is not directly addressable and ACLs can deny all access to the PE. This is the most secure option. If dynamic routing is used (RIP, OSPF, or BGP), the CE router must know the PE router's address, creating one potential attack point. Access to the PE router can be limited by ACLs to only the required routing protocol. Potential attacks include sending excessive routes or flooding with routing updates, which could cause denial of service but not unauthorized access.

To defend against these attacks, the PE router should accept only routing protocol packets from the CE router. MD5 authentication can be configured for BGP, OSPF, and RIP to prevent spoofed routing messages. The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) should be used where supported. Maximum prefix limits should be enforced, and route damping should be enabled. These measures limit attacks to the routing protocol itself, against which BGP has built-in protections like prefix filtering and damping.
sections.plainLanguage: Even if someone knows your network exists, they can only reach the one address where your network talks to theirs. If you use extra protection like password-protected routing and limits on how many routes you accept, you are protected against all but the most basic attacks.

sections.title: Advanced Architectures and Limitations
sections.content:
Advanced BGP/MPLS architectures add complexity and must be carefully secured. Carriers' Carrier architecture allows a carrier's customer (another carrier) to send labeled packets through the carrier's network. The PE router must verify that the top label was distributed to that CE, preventing label spoofing at the interface. Packets underneath the top label remain local to the customer carrier's VPN.

Inter-provider connections can use three approaches: VRF-to-VRF connections where each provider's PE treats the other as a CE; EBGP redistribution of labeled VPN-IPv4 routes; or PE-to-PE label exchange with ASBRs carrying only PE loopback addresses. All inter-provider solutions require trust between providers. A malicious provider could introduce packets into other providers' VPNs if it knows the label. The RFC specifies that such connections should only be made on private interconnection points.

BGP/MPLS IP VPNs do not protect against misconfiguration of the core network. An incorrectly configured PE router could leak traffic between VPNs. The architecture assumes the core is secure. If protection against attacks within the core is required, IPsec should be run over the MPLS infrastructure at least from CE to CE. The architecture also does not provide built-in encryption or integrity protection for data (encryption must be overlaid), and it does not address security of the customer network itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Connecting multiple providers is possible but risky; it requires each provider to trust the others completely. The architecture also does not protect against mistakes in how the network is set up, so those must be checked by the operators.
